clinicalPearls: Idiopathic granulomatous orchitis is a rare non-infective inflammatory condition that characteristically mimics a testicular tumour, usually in middle-aged men
It presents as a firm, sometimes tender, testicular mass or diffuse enlargement, often with a preceding history of trauma or infection
Germ cell tumour markers are normal, but this does not reliably distinguish it from a testicular tumour, so malignancy remains the primary concern
Ultrasound findings are non-specific and may resemble a neoplasm, and the diagnosis is frequently only made on histology after orchidectomy
It is a diagnosis of exclusion once specific granulomatous causes such as tuberculosis, other infections, and sarcoidosis have been considered
Because a tumour cannot be confidently excluded preoperatively, many patients undergo radical inguinal orchidectomy, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Where diagnosis can be established without radical surgery, anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive treatment may be considered, but tumour must first be excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic granulomatous orchitis is thought to represent an autoimmune or hypersensitivity reaction to extravasated sperm antigens, sometimes following trauma, infection, or obstruction that breaches the blood-testis barrier. The exposed germ cell antigens provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response within the seminiferous tubules and interstitium, with destruction of the tubules and formation of a firm mass. By definition, no specific infective organism or systemic granulomatous disease is identified, and the resulting swelling can closely imitate a testicular neoplasm.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumour of the testis
Other infective granulomatous orchitis (e.g. fungal, brucellosis)
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound to characterise the mass and assess the epididymis
Serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH (typically normal) to help assess for germ cell tumour
Urinalysis, culture, and tests for tuberculosis and other infections
Investigations for sarcoidosis when clinically suggested
Radical inguinal orchidectomy with histology when malignancy cannot be excluded
Histopathological review to confirm non-specific granulomatous inflammation
redFlags: Features indistinguishable from a testicular tumour on examination and imaging
Rapidly enlarging or hard testicular mass
Systemic symptoms suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy
Constitutional upset or nodal enlargement raising concern for lymphoma
reference.prognosis: The condition itself is benign, but because it cannot be reliably distinguished from malignancy preoperatively, the affected testis is often removed; once a tumour is excluded and specific causes treated, the prognosis is good, though the involved testis is frequently rendered non-functional by the inflammation.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign inflammatory cause and delaying exclusion of a testicular tumour
Relying on normal tumour markers to rule out malignancy
Failing to exclude tuberculosis and other specific granulomatous causes before labelling it idiopathic
Attempting conservative management before a tumour has been confidently excluded
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy, which is usually both diagnostic and therapeutic because a testicular tumour cannot be reliably excluded preoperatively
Exclude and treat specific granulomatous causes first, including tuberculosis with anti-tuberculous therapy, other infections, and sarcoidosis
Give a trial of antibiotics where an infective epididymo-orchitis element is present
Obtain serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) and scrotal ultrasound as part of the malignancy work-up
Confirm non-specific granulomatous inflammation on histopathology after surgery
Refer to urology, assess the contralateral testis, and counsel regarding fertility and hypogonadism after orchidectomy
